newsitem.title: USA: Hard to make El Nino crop predictions -- USDA.
newsitem.headline: Hard to make El Nino crop predictions -- USDA.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department's chief meteorologist on Thursday cautioned against drawing too strong a conclusion about the affect that an El Nino weather pattern could have on world crops this year.
"I would recommend anyone making a forecast on crop yields (based on the presence of the El Nino) to be very, very careful," meteorologist Albert Peterlin told Reuters.
Peterlin serves on USDA's World Agricultural Outlook Board, which issues new production forecasts each month on crops around the world.
While long-term weather forecasting has improved signficantly in recent years, it remains difficult to predict what impact El Nino will have on individual crops, he said.
El Nino refers to an increase in Pacific Ocean temperatures that typically triggers drier-than-normal conditions in Australia and weaker-than-normal monsoons in India and Southeast Asia.
Ninos occur every two to seven years and "without a doubt" the presence of one this year increases the chance that dryness could stunt the Australian wheat crop, Peterlin said.
But that crop, which will be harvested in December, has gone into its winter "dormancy" period in good shape thanks to adequate soil moisture, he said.
Even if El Nino causes drier-than-normal conditions, the crop could still be "just fine" if it receives only "one or two timely rainfalls" over the next 2 or 3 months, he said.

USDA has forecast the 1997/98 Australian wheat crop at 18.5 million tonnes, down sharply from 23.50 million last year. The decline reflects reduced plantings after a drop in prices, rather than concern over drought.
